newsitem.title: UK: KfW sets new benchmark in 10-year Euromark sector.
newsitem.headline: KfW sets new benchmark in 10-year Euromark sector.

text.p: German government agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW) launched a 2.0 billion mark 10-year Eurobond on Monday, setting a new benchmark.
The deal was snapped up by institutional investors hungry for the relative safety of mark assets as a result of continued uncertainty around European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
A move towards top-rated assets following sharp spread widening in emerging market bonds last week also helped the deal, traders said.

"In Europe investors have turned to marks as a safe haven, and KfW, rated triple-A, is a high-quality product which went well in the current environment," an official at joint lead manager Merrill Lynch said.
Dresdner Kleinwort Benson was the other lead manager.

"Given some of the question marks which have arisen again regarding EMU, it is a good time to offer a mark deal to European investors. We have seen particularly good interest from French and Dutch investors," the Merrill official said.
Profit-taking and spread widening last week in the high-yielding emerging market bond sector had led some investors to re-focus on the high-quality end of the market, he added.
Around 25 percent of Merrill Lynch's bonds were sold to Asian investors, who were attracted to the KfW deal because it was a straightforward mark bond.

"This is the first mark bond in a while without any euro features. Asian investors have a limited understanding of European markets, and have stayed away from recent bonds with tranches in guilders, French francs and marks because they were not sure which would perform better," the Merrill official said.
Some European borrowers, like Austria, the European Investment Bank and Siemens, have launched deals since January with clauses allowing for redenomination into euros.
Tranches in different currencies then become fungible to create a liquid euro Eurobond. Under plans for EMU, the single currency is due to be introduced on January 1, 1999.
"KfW will do what Germany does. If Germany redenominates its debt into euros, KfW will follow," the Merrill official said.

KfW bonds are considered a close substitute for German Bunds. Like Germany, KfW has a zero capital risk weighting. KfW paper pays a slight premium, with Monday's deal priced at 12 basis points over the January 2007 Bund. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7748
